opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that I come at this more from the language and representation side than as someone who builds game engines, but I think the question gets at something important.

My instinct is that visual quality is the easier thing to be impressed by, and the easier thing to be fooled by. We've seen this repeatedly with generative models. With text, fluent prose made people think a system understood more than it did. With video and world models it's the same: a beautiful, coherent-looking frame sequence is very persuasive, but it doesn't tell you whether the model has a usable model of the world.

For games specifically, what matters is whether the world responds correctly and consistently to what the player does. If I walk through a door, turn around, and walk back, is the room still there and the same? If I pick something up, does it stay picked up? Do the rules hold, so that a player can form expectations, plan, and be rewarded for skill? That's what gameplay is. It's about controllability, persistence, and causal consistency over long horizons, not about any single frame looking good.

So I'd weight gameplay much more heavily, and I'd evaluate it with interaction rather than passive viewing. Put agents or human players in the world, give them goals, and measure whether their actions have the predicted effects, whether state persists, and whether the experience stays coherent after many steps rather than drifting. Visual quality is a reasonable secondary criterion, and of course it matters for whether anyone wants to play. But plenty of great games have had very modest graphics. Very few have survived having rules that don't hold together.

The deeper point is that the interesting scientific question is whether these systems learn something like a structured, compositional model of the world, objects, agents, and causes, rather than a very good texture predictor. Gameplay-based evaluation probes that much more directly than looking at pretty pixels does.

r001.rationale: The response treats visual quality and gameplay quality as distinct evaluation dimensions, emphasizing gameplay while describing visual quality as a secondary criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd actually push back a little on the framing, because I think visual quality is the thing people get seduced by and it's mostly the wrong thing to be grading. The demos look stunning, and that's precisely why you have to be suspicious of them. What I care about is whether the thing is actually a model of a world, which means: does it have consistent state? If I walk around a corner and come back, is the room the same room? If I put down an object and leave for thirty seconds, is it still there? Does cause and effect hold up, so that when I push on something, the consequences follow and persist rather than dissolving into something that just looks plausible frame by frame?

That's really what gameplay is testing. A game is a set of rules and state that you can interact with, and a model that produces gorgeous imagery but has a sort of amnesia about its own world is, from a gameplay standpoint, broken, no matter how good the frames look. Conversely, something that looks like a 1996 PlayStation title but maintains coherent, controllable, rule-following state is genuinely much more interesting and much closer to being useful.

So if I had to put rough weights on it, I'd say coherence and controllability are maybe eighty percent of the judgment and visuals are the remainder, with the caveat that the visual stuff tends to improve fairly predictably with scale, whereas the state and causality problems are, I think, the hard research problems. There's a nice parallel to language models here. Early on, people were impressed that the text was fluent, and fluency turned out to be the easy part. The hard part was whether the model actually tracked what was being said and could reason about it. World models for games are in the fluency phase right now, and I'd want evaluations that look past it.

r001.rationale: The response treats visual quality and gameplay quality as distinct dimensions, contrasting visual appearance with coherent, controllable gameplay.

astra-6.text:
I’d put a lot of weight on gameplay, because a beautiful video isn’t necessarily a good world model. The important question is whether the world responds coherently to what you do. Can you move around, interact with objects, and have those actions produce consequences that persist?

Visual quality matters, of course. But if a game looks spectacular and the rules change every few seconds, you can’t really form a plan or learn to play it. I’d be more impressed by a visually simpler world with consistent mechanics, where you can predict what will happen and then test that prediction through your actions. That’s a much stronger demonstration of modeling a world than producing convincing frames.

r001.rationale: The response treats gameplay and visual quality as distinct evaluation dimensions, emphasizing coherent interaction and mechanics for gameplay while separately acknowledging how the world looks.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d put more weight on gameplay, although visual quality certainly matters. A world can look extraordinary in a short clip, but the real test is what happens when you interact with it. Do your actions have consistent consequences? Do objects persist? Can you learn how the world works and use that knowledge to accomplish something?

For games, you also need to distinguish visual realism from a coherent visual style. A game can be visually simple and still be wonderfully engaging. What’s harder to forgive is a world that looks realistic but changes its rules whenever you turn around. So I’d judge the model over sustained interaction: does it maintain a coherent world, and does that world support interesting decisions?

r001.rationale: It treats visual quality and gameplay as distinct considerations, weighing gameplay more heavily while noting that visual quality still matters.
